history.heading: Guaraní and Jesuits
paragraphs: Paraguay, a landlocked country in the heart of South America, was home to the Guaraní and other indigenous peoples. Spanish explorers founded Asunción in 1537, one of the oldest cities in South America. Spanish settlers and Guaraní mixed, creating a mestizo society.

Jesuit missionaries established missions (reductions) for the Guaraní in the 17th and 18th centuries, organising them into self-sufficient communities until the Jesuits were expelled in 1767. The ruins of La Santísima Trinidad de Paraná and Jesús de Tavarangue are UNESCO sites.

history.heading: Independence and catastrophic wars
paragraphs: Paraguay became independent in 1811. José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia ruled as dictator until 1840, isolating the country. Under the López family, Paraguay modernised but entered the War of the Triple Alliance (1864–1870) against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay. It was one of the deadliest wars in Latin American history: Paraguay lost a large share of its population, perhaps more than half, including most adult men.

Paraguay won the Chaco War against Bolivia (1932–1935). General Alfredo Stroessner ruled as dictator from 1954 to 1989, one of the longest dictatorships in Latin America. Democracy was restored afterwards.

culture.heading: A bilingual nation
paragraphs: Paraguay is unique in the Americas in that an indigenous language, Guaraní, is spoken by most of the population, alongside Spanish; both are official. Most people are Catholic.

Ñandutí lace, harp music and polka paraguaya are national traditions. Tereré, a cold herbal tea shared from a cup, is recognised by UNESCO. Chipa (cheese bread) and sopa paraguaya (a solid cornbread) are staples. Football is the most popular sport.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Paraguay is a presidential republic with a single five-year presidential term and a bicameral Congress. The conservative Colorado Party has governed for most of the past 75 years, including under Stroessner; Santiago Peña became president in 2023. Paraguay is one of few countries that recognise Taiwan.

economy.heading: Agriculture and hydropower
paragraphs: Paraguay is a major exporter of soybeans and beef. It generates far more electricity than it uses, thanks to the giant Itaipú dam shared with Brazil and the Yacyretá dam with Argentina, and exports the surplus. Re-export trade and a growing manufacturing sector (maquilas) are also important.
Paraguay has low taxes and stable growth, but inequality, informality and deforestation of the Chaco are challenges. The currency is the guaraní.
